No puzzles to solve but you do have to click the mouse to move the story along. It will make you think but it wont make you care. I dont regret the 9 hours I put into this game.

Orwell is a really solid visual novel. The plot is engrossing, with the right number of twists and player choice moments to keep things fresh over it's 5 episodes. Some enjoyable ambient music gives Orwell some much-needed atmosphere.

One slight disappointment was the gameplay, or at least player input in the game. While there are a few moments where your actions directly affect the plot, for the most part it is a case of finding the right entry or 'datachunk' in a given document to keep the story moving. It is extremely linear in that regard. For the purposes of the plot that is no bad thing, although it should be pointed out that the game itself has less player input than advertsied.

At £7.19 I was a bit disappointed with the game's length. Less than 3 and a half hours was enough for me to finish the story: I felt like I read most/all entries in that time, and did not feel I was rushing.

In a sale, I recommend Orwell for a good plot and treatment of surveillance issues. Be prepared for the game to influence you, though, rather than you influencing it.
definitely recommend.

Absolutely recommend the game. If you get into it - and if you are attentive, you will - you will be faced with moral dilemmas which are very fun to experience. The good sides are a captivating, neat story which provokes thoughts regarding the real world, especially mass surveillance. It's not entirely presented as black-and-white, either, which is always a bonus. You understand that the Orwell system can be very useful against any crime, but that it has unparalleled capacity for abuse, as well. Without giving spoilers, that's all I can say.

The one thing which irked me was the difficulty of distinguishing between what datachunks are necessary, and which ones are not. While I wouldn't have an issue with this, the judgements you make can have consequences. ...Hey, that's actually a good thing!

Definitely recommend. Even has replay value.

Great game! Very interesting story craft. Nice take on mass surveillance and law.

Can be frustrating to find the clues to trigger the next chapter. But overall good!

8.5/10

This helps Snowden's case as much as John Oliver d*ck pic report. You start with digging through public information, and then quickly slip into the private data of people with the slightest connection to the target. Because, hey, your handler told you that a judge gave you a warrant, right?

Finished in 3 hours, did not replay to look for alternate choices.

You play as a character who works for the government and has complete access to internet, phone calls, text messages, etc. Your job is to investigate people, collect evidence, and solve (and prevent) terrorist crimes. You're the man behind the camera in the all-seeing surveillance state. 

The way the surveillance system is set up is that you collect the information and pass it to an analyst. The analyst looks at the information and decides whether it is sufficient to arrest somebody, or enough to indicate another person is a person of interest that you're allowed to investigate. Over time the network of people you're investigating grows, and it's harder to keep track of their history and relationionships.

If you collect the correct information, you might be able to prevent terrorist attacks. It is possible to get enough evidence to arrest people who aren't actually dangerous or ringleaders.

Sometimes, you see conflicting information (such as when one person is lying) and you need to make a decision. You can't submit both pieces of evidence, you can't delete evidence once you've submitted it (silly, but a game mechanic to make your choices more meaningful), and sometimes it's not clear which one is correct. You sometimes can dig around and find out which piece is correct, but sometimes you need to go with your gut and what you think the people's motivations are. 

Other times, it's not clear that you're making a choice. You can always choose to submit or not submit information, and it could lead to different results. The only way to know this is to replay the game and deliberately not choose things that led to bad outcomes. At first I was just grabbing and submitting all the information I saw, but you're intended to put a bit more thought into it. Is this relevent information? Do you want the analyist making a decision based on this information? Is this quote being taken out of context? Are you encouraging your analyist to arrest a harmless person?

My only complaint about the game is [spoiler] there is only one case/group you get to investigate, and that investigation turns "meta" at the end -- having discovered the ORWELL system you're using to spy on them, they start interacting with you directly. I kind of wanted to see the system working as intended for a few cases before the "finale" case where your subjects figure out what's going on.[/spoiler] I know it's a smaller indie type of game, but a few more cases to establish what you're doing, how significant your choices are, and so on BEFORE it reached that point would have been appreciated.

I did enjoy this game. It involves a lot of reading, and a lot of thinking, in order to enjoy it properly. It's not a good game for people who want to click through the boring stuff to get to the exciting part. In a way, it's more akin to the visual novel genre than it is to more traditional games.

Orwell is really good. For some reason I had the impression that the gameplay would involve procedurally generated scenarios, in which I'd have to "keep an eye on people" or for all you normal folk "stalk and invade the privacy of civilians". Instead Orwell focuses on a few seemingly connected terrorist attacks and street violence, therein you're tasked with finding the connection between the people involved with said crimes. You can indict people by using uninformed and speculative information. You could alternatively not give away incriminating evidence, which can have immediate and notable impact on the story. 

The driving force behind Orwell (and of course, George Orwell's 1984) is how information can be used and misused, on both a small and large scale. There's a heap of references to 1984 by the way, mostly names and terminology as to be expected. Considering this is Osmotic Studios' first release, I'm very impressed with the quality and depth to Orwell's story. The character interactions can sometimes be a bit unnatural but it's a very minor complaint. The user interface is very clean and simple to use. The plot is quite engrossing and there are a couple questions I was really intrigued to know the answer to. There's also a decent amount of non-pertinent information - either to mislead you down a rabbit hole or merely to let people explore some of the finer, less necessary details of the characters in the story. Either way I tried to read most of it, and found the vast majority of the writing to be solid and interesting. Even some of the joke articles are absurd and enjoyable to read. Also, the music is generally very quiet & subtle, only picking up when a big reveal happens. Was simple, but a very nice touch.

All in all, I think Orwell is a great, unique story presented very well. The gameplay elements help to keep it engaging and involved too. Easy recommendation.
Great game 10/10.

Orwell is a game that really makes you question the game itself.  Who is the bad guy here?

You play an investigator using the government's new tool in testing, called Orwell.  You basically use an in-game browser to do research on people to determine if they are responsible for criminal activity.  The execution of this is pretty good, and the story that ties everything together is pretty intricate.  

While there is a lot of reading and linearity, there are also plenty of moments where you directly effect the outcome, and I can see myself playing the game at least one more time to try for different results and maybe a "better" ending.  My first play through took about 3 hours.

The graphics are simplistic, but they work well.  The music is really good though and definitely helps set the mood.

I received Orwell as part of Humble Monthly, but I do feel I got a great amount of enjoyment out of it, and I feel it's worth the $9.99 it's currently priced.

Orwell is a genius game putting the player in the very unique position of being an intelligence officer. It focuses on the 21st century question of information freedom versus national security. It gives you a lot of responsibility in decision making and makes you question yourself. The story is very interesting and the visual communication is perfectly executed. I highly recommend it to anybody who is looking for something with a little more meaning!

Orwell is a slow game but by no means relaxing. It's kind of a detective-spy-game with heavy emphasis on decision-making and filtering important information. In principle the gameplay only consists of reading texts and passing certain information pieces to your boss.
Even though the transitions between the "stages" of the game are pretty smooth and understandable, I could not help noticing the more or less strict storyline, which you have to follow. Once you have passed the right information new pages and conversations are unlocked, providing new information. If you do not pass anything, nothing happens.

I didn't like mainly two things:

-Conflicting information. Two sets of information which are said to be contradictory. But I had some cases in which they weren't. They even added up somehow and I would have liked to pass both, still I had to choose one.

-Your boss tells you to only pass important information but although he insults you if you pass nonsense it is not clear if anything happens at all. (But I must say, I did not exhaustibly try it out.)

I would guess, that the freedom of decision has not the impact, which the game wants you to believe it has. The ending seemed pretty prescribed, meaning you land there in any case, but maybe some day I try it out again.

TL;DR : A very nice game, which is definitely worth a try, if you dont mind that this game wants to pretend to have a degree of freedom it possibly hasn't.

what a SUPERB game!!

I started it just to try it out and give it a go (I got it in the monthly humble) but I found myself so much attached to it I had to finish it all in two sessions!

The game plays out like a detective game, it feels mostly passive because the only thing you can do except reading the events is to gather infos and try to make them as much reliable as possible to the context. the "choice matters" is absolutely present, but at the same time it's not clear when it happens, which is good. no more "the character will remember that" (you hear me telltale??).

There are two things though I disliked. First, what you gather is mostly final, especially with conflicting chunks. I understand what they're doing here, by forcing you to investigate on your own properly before giving out an answer, but sometimes data is ambivalent (one character thinks something, another the opposite with no factual truth in between but just speculation on how you see it) or just ambiguous. Then, when it's uploaded, it's done. Other times you upload things and your advisor jumps to conclusions or take the information literally or completely out of context, some other times they give a background to it. It's very inconsistent and it made me feel "will it understand correctly the meaning of this upload?"

Second, - I will keep it spoiler free - and this one has been a big one for me, there's no neutral ending. At least none that I could find. You can either be the gov's dog by forging evidence, or the rebellious revolutionary that destroyed the system. No in-between. 
This will probably trigger somebody, but I found Orwell a decent tool for investigations, while the whole game continuously point at it as inherently bad, so if you support it you must be bad. I think no tools are good or bad, it's how we use them and we can see it in this game the ethical modifications done to it have improved it by far. It has flaws, true, (especially if you give the tool to an untrained person treating it as a game... what the heck, seriously.) but all in all if the system is actually restricted to investigate actual threats it could be an interesting way to manage it. We all had to deal with terrorists lately unfortunately, and we all cry for help and for prevention. This might be another tool to help us. 

So I don't get why you HAVE to be bad if you support it? Why can't you just incriminate the bombers and call it a day? why do you need to fabricate evidence or else being called disobedient and incriminate yourself? Very bummed by this choice in the climax of the ending.

I'm honestly surprised by how deep of an experience Orwell was. 

I felt that I had a pretty strong take on the game I thought I was about to play going into it, and for the most part I did. I thought I would be combing through fake social media and what not looking for clues to help unlock whatever comes next. I figured this would be a slightly different take on "A Normal Lost Phone." 

What I didn't expect at all was a pretty deep story and somewhat relatable characters. It's pretty impressive that this story was able to be told without feeling stiff or crammed down your throat. There were people I hated and those I felt sorry for. No matter what decision I made, it always felt like the wrong one. I felt like a part of the problem which was very much by design. The writers deserve a ton of credit for the impact of Orwell. 

Orwell, as a game, I could best liken to a visual novel. There aren't any real puzzles or keys to unlocking what comes next. For the most part this is just grabbing info and putting it into the right folder to progress the story, which the game makes it impossible to screw up. There is a great deal of decision making which I have to guess can greatly alter the story. It's hard to say without subsequent play-throughs, but I was very satisfied with how my one and only play went. The only thing I'd love to see is the ability to replay a day, especially the last since I feel like there are a lot branching story opportunities that you will miss in a single play. 

Overall this made me feel shady AF and I loved every minute. Can't wait to see what they do with the sequel. RECOMMEND!

I can't say I've played a game like this in a while or knew that games like this still existed.  It's almost a modern day "choose your own adventure." The game is thought provoking and a reminder that it is difficult to boil different perspectives down to a "truth." 
I didn't want to stop investigating, even when the game was over.  Would reccomend.

The reason I say I had a conflicted experience is because this game is focused on a semi realistic plot, but then there are a few bits that are technologically stupid (speaking as a software dev), I would have preferred sticking to the realism they portrayed. I also found the conflicting data chunks to be an unpleasing mechanic, as someone else mentioned it's difficult to make a choice when there's not enough information.

Despite the parts I disliked I persevered through it and ended up enjoying it overall, sadly only when trying to get the achievements on my second play through did I realise that not uploading data chunks can be a valid option in some situations.

And if any dev should read this, any game that uses a web browser feel to it should support using the mouse side buttons for forward/backward navigation and middle click for scrolling!! That was the first and most annoying thing I noticed with this game.

The message is clear, and although sometimes heavy-handedly delivered, merits consideration. And that is what this game really does: It makes you think.

Orwell is an investigative game akin to a visual novel. You play as The Investigator, someone whose job it is to use the powerful Orwell surveillance system to solve crimes – or in this case, solve a particular crime. You see, a bomb was set off in Freedom Plaza in The Nation, killing three people, and it is your job to try and catch the bomber before they can kill anyone else.

Orwell is more like an interactive novel than an ordinary video game – the game is wholly centered around reading text for about four and a half hours, and while it has more meaningful interaction than most visual novels, the actual gameplay itself is very simple and not very action-oriented. It is a very cerebral experience, and if reading lots of text isn’t your cup of tea, this is not the game for you.

You start out with a single person of interest – a young woman who left the Plaza shortly before the bomb went off. She was a protester who had been arrested for attacking a police officer, but who wasn’t prosecuted for it due to lack of evidence. It quickly becomes clear that not all is as it seems, and it seems unlikely that she personally was the bomber – but she has past associations with a group known as Thought, an anti-government group which often engages in extremist rhetoric. But are they really the sort of people who would kill people? Or are they just innocent bystanders coincidentally caught up in the investigation?

Orwell is a very ambiguous game, and it is precisely this ambiguity which really makes the game work. Thought is upset about living in a surveillance state, but it is clear from your perspective as The Investigator that the system is designed to be humane in many ways – the investigator passes on information to someone else, whose job it is to analyze the data. You cannot investigate people who aren’t targets – unless someone has been designated as suspicious by actual data, you cannot collect data at all them, nor are you allowed to go snooping through their things. But if they are a target of interest, you have nigh unlimited authority to go snooping. And while the state is clearly a bit authoritarian, it is also clear that the system works – crime has gone down, and you can catch several criminals over the course of the game who really did do bad things. The person on the other end, who helps to determine whether or not the data is really indicative of wrongdoing, is a genuinely nice person who cares about people and who urges you to collect more data. The leader of The Nation appears to genuinely be trying to help out neighboring states.

But all of this is muddied with the ambiguity of the fact that not everyone in the government is nice, and the general sinister nature of your surveillance. Your actions do have consequences, and it is clear that if you made the wrong decisions, you could potentially feed people bad data and get people put in jail – and the choice of whether or not to feed people bad data, and the impression you leave the government on people, is dependent on what data you give them.

The game, thus, is a combination of an investigation and a moral choice system – you are not only investigating who might be the bomber, but also deciding what is and is not relevant, what should and should not be part of the investigation, and you have the power to wrongfully put people in jail or put people in danger. The very simple gameplay of choosing what pieces of highlighted information to put into a database from various documents, webpages, emails, and phone and text conversations thus takes on a great deal of weight, and makes you think about what you’re doing in a very different way from other investigatory games, as you think of it not only in terms of true/false, but also whether the information morally belongs in the hands of the government.

The game’s gameplay also shows how a system like that can lead to paranoia, as you see people engage in a lot of extremist rhetoric and it is easy to jump to conclusions and morally convict someone in your mind who didn’t do anything worse than complain, as well as how easy it is to prejudge someone in the opposite direction as well, making you think more positively of them than they truly deserve. And it puts stress on the player as well – you cannot take back your actions, so if you incorrectly present someone as a dangerous criminal, you can’t fix it and have to live with the consequences.

How humane the system is – and who is in the right and wrong – is a complicated question that the game ultimately doesn’t answer for itself, but which the player answers via their actions throughout the game. Like “The Lady or the Tiger”, the way the player responds to the story really reflects as much on the player’s own evaluation of humanity, and how they weigh the risks and benefits of a system like that. Rather than being preachy about how evil the system is, the game also shows why people might like a system like that and want it to be implemented. It is perhaps the most even-handed presentation of the subject matter I’ve seen, and it achieves this by putting the player in the seat of someone who might be a part of such a system and showing just how ambiguous the system can be and how much power they wield, both how dangerous it can be if misused but how beneficial it can be if used appropriately.

It has some new concepts thrown in which are nice but the content within is very limited (the game ends just as you start getting the ability to do cool stuff with Orwell) and even though there seems to be some replay value within I don't feel particularly compelled to go through all of it again. I think the idea is just too hard to realize properly as a game. I'd certainly doesn't work for me in this game.

Though provoking and surprisingly tense at times. You take the role of an government investigator, working with limited information, to paint the correct picture for your advisor. He can only see the information you share, and picking the correct, most likely version, of the truth is your responsibility. Screw up and people could die.

On a philosophical level, Orwell really opens the question of liberty vs. protection. How far is too far?

The game involves searching various (in-game) webpages to find information about suspected terrorists.  You get to decide what information to share with authorities and what to withhold, which affects the outcome.

It's decently fun.  There's about 4-5 hours of content.  If you enjoy Uplink you'll probably enjoy this.

Cool general concept which is severely undermined by the fact that all choices are final - which makes absolutely no sense in a computer system of any kind. This is just an artificial way to "up the stakes" but this is incredibly transparent and lazy. In fact, whatever initial immersion I got from the experience was broken as soon as I realized the above fact - no real-world system would behave this way, and I'm back to just playing a video game.

What's worse, is that there IS a "chapter select" feature, which is completely locked until you complete the game (so you can't even restart the chapter you've already played through)...

I love the game but it has some quirks.
1. Like some others, I believe that 'conflicting data chunks' should be revisable after entry pending new evidence.  The 'Test Case' has two personality traits that could both be true... or neither.  You have to choose one.
2. Is that... a bug?  Further into Test Case you need to find the full name of a Person of Interest.  I spent 10 minutes digging and digging through all available documents and found ONE listing of the name (immediately, actually) but it wasn't highlighted as a valid and usable Data Chunk.  Literally NOTHING else anywhere on this guy's name.  (Either I hardcore dumbed it up here or there's a bug regarding this Data Chunk.)
3. Restrictive Data Chunk gathering.  I recognized/found quite a bit of relevant data in documents but wasn't able to enter/drag-drop it as a Data Chunk into the appropriate Person of Interest's file... just because it didn't want me to worry about that yet?

Of course, I was just under an hour into the game and -mostly- (I think?) through the first 'Test' Case so issue #3 may just be a 'beginner' or tutorial-ish feature as it coaxes you into learning how to play without need of a cut-and-dry tutorial.  Overall, I say this game is definitely worth giving a try if you enjoy modern mysteries and actively uncovering the story for yourself.

For how low the budget for this must have been and fairly scarce interface, I think that this was really surprisingly well done with various ways to make it interesting. The story telling is mostly text-based and bases itself on the choices you make as you pick evidence. It has various political themes that are analyzed, and characters that seem quite realistic. 

It's a lot of fun to dig all of this "secret" information on the characters you are investigating. At times it really feels like violating their space. It feels quite uneasy at times with the background music changing at times quite suddenly when there is something a bit more revealing, but it fits well with the story telling. 

None of the characters were very likable though, even though that is probably never the main idea in it. Writing in that sense was pretty okay, even though it felt at times to be made by amateurs.

It's a fairly cheap game so I don't see any reason why you shouldn't try this if you like story driven games with freedom of choice. It's very captivating and easy to grasp and it gives you a lot to think about ethicality.

If you have heard nothing of this game and the general possible plot beats, please purchase this now. Please support these developers and their first masterpeice.

BACKGROUND

Got the game in the October Humble Monthly.

I'm not sure if I've played something like this before. The closest I can think of is Papers Please, but that feels like a slight stretch. 



TOTAL TIME PLAYING

Just over 3 hours. That was enough for me to personally beat the game. the average time on HLTB is 4 hours. 

SPECS FOR PLAY THROUGH 

- AMD FX 8350 @ 4.0 GHz
- GTX 1080
- 8 Gb DDR3 RAM @ 668 MHz
- 7200 RPM HDD
- LG Ultrawide

PERFORMANCE

The graphic style isn't demanding (that isn't to say it's a "bad" looking game). I was able to maintain full 60 FPS the entire time, and I'd be surprised if any modern day machine cannot do the same. 

PROS

+Amazing story. I played through this in two sittings and all I could think about in between the two sessions was going back and playing the rest. 
+ As soon as you start to feel overwhelmed with the massive influx in characters, the game ends. This could be viewed as a con, but I don't think a game like this would benefit from character-over-load. 
+ As I mentioned earlier, the graphics are pretty interesting. Everything has a flat look to it. Really interesting. 

CONS

 - Orwell does a lot right. Unfortunately, I feel like it held my hand far too much. Instead of looking through a wide range of documents, the game was constantly pushing me into specific documents. This would be super hard to work around, but towards the end the choices and clues became very obvious and the game lost it's "detective" feel it built up so well in the first half. 
- As far as I could tell, you can't get anything wrong. Sure some of the "conflicting evidence" could be misdiagnosed, but 
from my play-through adding useless information just got a sarcastic response from your boss. No real consequences. 
CONCLUSION

Alright. So I really liked the game. It was great and a pretty phenomenal gaming experience. At this time I am going to recommend it if found on sale around $5. It's far too short to be worth $10. 

I'm really hoping a sequel or an entire new story comes out. With that new game I really want the choices to be less linear. Hold my hand less, let me mess things up, and let things pivot around my mistakes.

I would recommend this game, but not to everyone. If you enjoy dystopian settings and stories, this game gives you a unique perspective in that this time you are Big Brother's informant. You spy on civilians and you decide what information to pass along.

This game is a lot of reading and linking bits of information together. It is not very action packed, though there is plenty going on to read about. Getting a handle on the controls is pretty straightforward and easy. It makes you have to decide what kind of person you want to be: one who follows orders and sticks to the rules, one who picks and chooses what rules they want to follow, or one that defies orders and stands for their own beliefs.

My biggest complaint is that the story felt somewhat short. It is designed to feel like the events are happening in "real time" as you play, but I feel like there was a lot of background that could have been brought forward and utilized to extend the story a bit. Overall, though, the story as it stands is still pretty intriguing.

If you're an achievement hunter, they are all easy enough to get in a few playthroughs. One playthrough took me I think around 5-6 hours, and that was taking my time deciding what I wanted to do.

Thought provoking, compelling and very relevent to our modern world.

Basically the book 1984 as a wonderful made game. A wonderful visual novel with some decisions especially towards the end. As a german, with both Nazi, Stasi past and the current Netzdg, one starts thinking which social network is really necessary.

Here's the situation: you have been selected by The Nation (a fictitious country) to test drive this super-secret surveliance program called Orwell. You have the power to snoop up lives of the citizens, be nosy on everything, and read, listen, and access the very personal lives of the people, just for the sake of security. You do trust yourself their data will be in your good hands, but how will you prove your intention?

Orwell depicts that very feeling of handling all the data from the citizens by reading everything on the (fictitious) internet, ranging from news articles, blog posts, to private messages and transcribed phone calls. You are supposed to look for information regarding to crime only, but would you? What information will you extract? Who do you think this person is, by looking behind the screen of Orwell only?

Speaking of reading contents, I can assure you those contents are meticulously written, since the game is based on reading them. They did not just throw in words to make them look like it, but they feel so real as if in real lives. News articles, blog posts, social media posts, even chatlogs look so real. Even typos on chatlogs look so real. I am a nosy person myself, so snooping around the lives of people by reading these "real" stuffs feels like scratching an itch away.

That being said, this game is not that perfect. You should get ready to read everything in order to enjoy the game. If you love reading everything on the internet, especially in English, this game is definitely for you. If not, you will find yourself in the hell full of words and nothing else. You won't see many graphics or anything other than Orwell's clean interface. Every event unveils through the interface only, as if you're sitting in front of your PC (which you are) watching something happening out there through words.

Also, there are some nasty bugs when trying to replay the game for achievements, and I hope the devs will fix them. Please don't let this great game sunk down by nasty bugs!
